title: Why Canada invested in Cohere | BetaKit
html:
Today we have another edition of what is becoming a quarterly accountability check-in with Canada’s AI Minister, Evan Solomon.

“Simply put, Canada is not gonna wait for others to build the AI—maybe people we don’t know or don’t trust. We’re gonna build it now.”

The last time the minister was on the podcast, it was shortly following the release of Canada’s AI strategy. This time, we’re checking in right after Budget 2026, and we talk through some of the budget components the minister is most passionate about in their support of entrepreneurs. We also cover how some of those steps are designed to help prevent more AI companies like Taalas and Tenstorrent from being acquired or fleeing south—for his part, Minister Solomon said it’s his job to give those companies reasons not to leave.

But we also talk about the big news that dropped right before the budget: the federal government’s investment in AI champion Cohere. If you’ve seen the minister on The BetaKit Podcast before, or are familiar with BetaKit’s coverage generally, this news should not surprise you.

But public investments in private companies are relatively novel in Canada, and now that every Canadian has skin in the game, they’re coming armed with a lot of questions. As Build Canada’s Lucy Hargreaves put it, “Ottawa is becoming the owner, the funder, the customer and the regulator of the same companies.” How is that going to work?

I put the question to the minister directly alongside these two: why did the feds choose this approach, and how much can Canadians expect to know about their growing tech portfolio?

Do you want to know the answers? Let’s dig in.
